newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bitter charges fly in French election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Bitter charges fly in French election campaign.

text.p: France's election campaign is turning bitter with charges of complacency over the far right flying between the ruling conservatives and the Socialists, seen losing ground nine days from the snap poll's first round.

National Front leader Jean-Marie Le Pen urged far-rightists to back the left in the June 1 run-off in order to derail President Jacques Chirac's plans to take France into the euro single currency and build a Europe that, he said, would make "Hitler's dream come true".

Gaullist ex-budget minister Nicolas Sarkozy voiced surprise on Thursday that Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin and his lieutenants "had not firmly rejected, in the name of morality, Le Pen's vibrant appeal to vote for them".
Le Pen said a leftist election victory could also help his cause by paralysing the country and forcing another snap election in a year with the Front better placed than now.
An infuriated Jospin warned the right not to taunt the left about the National Front, an anti-immigrant party held at arm's length by all mainstream parties.

"If anything has to be clarified, it is on the side of the right...If there is any leakage, it is between the ideas of the far-right and the right, never with the left's ideas," he told a Paris rally of some 5,000 young people.
He recalled that the Front's number two, Bruno Megret, was a former Gaullist and that Nice mayor Jacques Peyrat had left the Front for the Gaullist RPR party.

"If you open (Interior Minister) Debre's fridge, you will find Mr Megret in the freezer and Mr Peyrat among fresh products," he said. Debre, in rhetoric akin to the Front's, recently charged that immigrants were emptying the French people's refrigerators.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe, campaigning in his hometown Bordeaux, accused the Socialists of using "wicked and vicious soundbites to conceal the emptiness of their thought".
He said the left's plans to increase wages would bankrupt tens of thousands of small and medium-sized businesses and ruin a trend to curb record unemployment.

He said that Jospin had been forced by his election alliance with the Communists to take positions that would be disastrous for Europe if he came to power as Communists "oppose not only the euro but the very principle of European construction".
The Socialists, while backing the single European currency, propose relaxing the Maastricht budget criteria to make the fight against unemployment the priority.

The latest opinion poll, by Ipsos, said the centre-right would retain a clear majority with 323 seats -- up from 290 a week ago -- to the combined left's 293. The National Front was seen winning only one of 577 seats in the National Assembly.

Social unrest broke into the election campaign with farmers dumping tonnes of fruit in several cities to protest against cheap imports, a train controllers strike threatening to ruin a long holiday weekend for tens of thousands, and airline pilots vowing to stop work for four days next week.
Juppe acknowledged social discontent but warned disgruntled conservatives against being tempted to cast protest votes in the first round and go fishing instead of voting in the run-off.
"Such behaviour, get this well into your head, could return Socialism to power," he said.
